ADDED i1: Tests {@link StringSubstitutor}'s handling of complex escaping.

The escape character is {@code $}. Writing it twice ({@code $$}) emits a single literal {@cod
ADDED i2: Variable name to value mappings shared by every substitution in this test.
ADDED i4: Longer, more realistic variables.
ADDED i6: "$$" escapes the leading "$" so the outer "${...}" survives as literal text, while the inner variable is still substituted.
ADDED i7: Both "$" characters of the inner "${...}" are escaped, so nothing inside is substituted and the whole inner expression is emitted literally.
ADDED i8: Surrounding literal text (leading/trailing dots) is preserved verbatim.
ADDED i9: The "-" default-value syntax: "undefined.number" is unknown, so its default "1234567890" is used, then escaped into literal "${1234567890}".
ADDED i10: Substitutes {@code template} with a {@link StringSubstitutor} backed by {@link #values} and asserts the result equals {@code expectedResult} across every {@code
ADDED i11: When substring is requested, the inner portion of the template is expected to produce the inner portion of the result (first and last characters dropped).
